messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL from a piezo transducer.
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{out}$ (average) $\ge 4.5\text{V}$
        *   $V_{out}$ (max) $\le 5.5\text{V}$
        *   Ripple $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (50mV)
        *   Startup time $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$
        *   Settled $\Delta V \le 0.02\text{V}$
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ and $20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   $V_{OC}$ (amplitude) $\approx 3.8\text{V}$ at S1.
    *   Operating conditions: S1 to S6 (various loads and excitations).
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components, 4 switches, 2 SYNC controllers.
    *   Crucial observation: $V_{OC} \approx 3.8\text{V}$ is *less* than the required $V_{out} \ge 4.5\text{V}$. A simple rectifier (like the FBR reference) cannot boost the voltage. We need a DC-DC converter or an energy harvesting technique like SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor) or a boost converter.

    *   Standard Full-Bridge (FBR): Fails because it's passive. $V_{out} \approx V_{OC} - 2V_{diode}$.
    *   SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):
        *   SSHI flips the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks of the displacement, effectively increasing the voltage seen by the rectifier.
        *   Topology: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Storage. An inductor $L$ is switched across the piezo terminals at the peaks to invert the voltage.
    *   Boost Converter:
        *   Requires a switch and an inductor. Since the piezo is an AC source, we either rectify first then boost, or use a synchronous boost.
        *   Given the SYNC controller, an SSHI-like approach is very natural.

    *   *Option 1: Parallel-SSHI (P-SSHI)*
        *   Rectifier (Full Bridge) to charge $C_{out}$.
        *   A switch and inductor in parallel with the piezo to flip $V_{Cp}$ at peaks.
        *   Actually, P-SSHI usually puts the inductor in parallel with the piezo and switches it at the peaks.
    *   *Option 2: Series-SSHI (S-SSHI)*
        *   Inductor in series with the rectifier.
    *   *Option 3: Synchronous Rectification/Boost (Standard Boost)*
        *   Difficult with just 2 SYNC controllers and AC input.

    *   The "voltage flip" increases the average voltage extracted.
    *   Let's design a basic SSHI:
        *   Full bridge rectifier: $D_1(\text{pzp} \to \text{out})$, $D_2(\text{pzn} \to \text{out})$, $D_3(0 \to \text{pzp})$, $D_4(0 \to \text{pzn})$. Wait, the provided reference bridge is `["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`.
        *   Wait, if the bridge is connected as described:
            *   $D_1: \text{pzp} \to \text{out}$
            *   $D_2: \text{pzn} \to \text{out}$
            *   $D_3: 0 \to \text{pzp}$
            *   $D_4: 0 \to \text{pzn}$
            *   This is a full bridge.
        *   Now add the flipping circuit:
            *   An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$.
            *   $S$ connects the inductor $L$ across the piezo terminals (pzp and pzn) at the peaks.
            *   Circuit: Piezo terminals are `pzp` and `pzn`. We can put a switch $S$ and inductor $L$ in series, connected between `pzp` and `pzn`.
            *   Wait, the SYNC controller closes the switch. When the switch is closed, $L$ is in parallel with $C_p$. This causes an LC oscillation, flipping the voltage.
            *   $T_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ and $L = 10\text{mH}$, $T_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \times 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\text{\mu s}$. This fits the $1\text{\mu s}$ to $0.001\text{s}$ range.

    *   $V_{OC} = 3.8\text{V}$. With SSHI, we can potentially reach $V_{out} > V_{OC}$.
    *   However, the bridge rectifier has a voltage drop ($\sim 0.5\text{V}$ for DSCH).
    *   We need to reach $4.5\text{V}$ to $5.5\text{V}$.
    *   Let's try an SSHI topology:
        *   Full bridge (DSCH) to `out`.
        *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   $S$ controlled by `SYNC` (edges="both", phase=0).
        *   $C_{out}$ to filter.
        *   Zener diode $DZ33$ is only $3.3\text{V}$, so it's not useful for a $4.5\text{V}-5.5\text{V}$ target (it would clamp it too low). We need a way to keep it below $5.5\text{V}$ but above $4.5\text{V}$. A large $C_{out}$ and the load $R_L$ might be enough, but the requirements are tight ($\Delta V \le 0.02\text{V}$, ripple $\le 0.05\text{V}$).

    *   Is there a better way to boost? A charge pump?
    *   A switched-capacitor boost could work, but SYNC controllers are better suited for LC inversion.
    *   Let's look at the "reference design" again. It failed because $V_{out}$ was too low. SSHI is the classic solution for this.

    *   Rectifier:
        *   $D_1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
        *   $D_2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
        *   $D_3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
        *   $D_4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
    *   SSHI Flip:
        *   $L_1$: `pzp` $\to$ `n1`
        *   $S_1$: `n1` $\to$ `pzn`, ctrl: `G1`
        *   $G_1$: SYNC, edges: `both`, phase: `0`, $t_{on} \approx 50\text{\mu s}$.
    *   Storage:
        *   $C_1$: `out` $\to$ `0`, $2.2\text{\mu F}$ (starting point).

    *   S1: $I_p=60\text{uA}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=2.2\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Power available $\approx 0.5 \cdot C_p \cdot V_{OC}^2 \cdot f \approx 0.5 \cdot 25\text{nF} \cdot 3.8^2 \cdot 100 \approx 18\text{\mu W}$.
    *   Load power at $4.5\text{V} \approx 4.5^2 / 2.2\text{M} \approx 9.2\text{\mu W}$.
    *   S4 (weakest): $I_p=40\text{uA}, f=100\text{Hz}, R_L=4.7\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Power available $\approx 0.5 \cdot 25\text{nF} \cdot (40/60 \cdot 3.8)^2 \cdot 100 \approx 8\text{\mu W}$.
    *   Load power at $4.5\text{V} \approx 4.5^2 / 4.7\text{M} \approx 4.3\text{\mu W}$.
    *   SSHI can significantly increase efficiency, making these targets feasible.

    *   To avoid $V_{out} > 5.5\text{V}$ (especially in S3 where $R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega$), we might need a clamping mechanism. But a Zener at $3.3\text{V}$ is too low. A Zener at $5.1\text{V}$ would be perfect, but we only have `DZ33`.
    *   Wait, maybe a Zener chain? Or just rely on the load and a large $C_{out}$?
    *   Actually, the SYNC controller and the inductor $L$ can be used for a more advanced SSHI (like SEH), but let's start with P-SSHI.
    *   Let's consider a different topology for Design 2: A "Boost" approach using the SYNC controller.
        *   Instead of a full bridge, maybe a half-bridge with a boost inductor.
        *   But the simplest boost for a piezo is SSHI. Let's try a variation.

    *   *Design 1: P-SSHI*
        *   Rectifier (Full Bridge, DSCH)
        *   L-S switch in parallel with piezo.
        *   $C_{out}$ for storage.
    *   *Design 2: S-SSHI* (Inductor in series with the bridge)
        *   Rectifier (Full Bridge, DSCH)
        *   Inductor $L$ in series with the positive side of the bridge.
        *   Wait, S-SSHI usually involves switching the inductor. Let's stick to P-SSHI.
    *   *Design 3: Synchronous Rectification + Boost (simplified)*
        *   If I use switches instead of diodes for the bridge? (Limited to 4 switches).
        *   We can use 2 switches for the rectifier and 2 for the flip.
        *   $S_1$: `pzp` $\to$ `out`
        *   $S_2$: `pzn` $\to$ `out`
        *   $S_3$: `0` $\to$ `pzp`
        *   $S_4$: `0` $\to$ `pzn`
        *   But the SYNC controllers only provide two channels (`G1`, `G2`) and they are tied to the piezo extrema. This means $S_1/S_3$ would trigger at the same time as $S_2/S_4$. This is not how a rectifier works. A rectifier needs to be "on" for a half-period, not for a few microseconds.
        *   Correction: The SYNC controller closes the switch for $t_{on}$. This is only suitable for the "flip" (the LC oscillation), not for the rectification phase. So we *must* use diodes for the rectification.

    *   The "flip" happens at the peaks. $V_{pzp}$ is max, $S_1$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ oscillate, $V_{pzp}$ becomes min.
    *   This increases the voltage across the rectifier diodes.
    *   Wait, the reference bridge used `DSCH`. Let's use that.

    *   $C_{out}$ needs to be large enough to keep ripple $< 50\text{mV}$.
    *   $I_{load} \approx 4.5\text{V} / 2.2\text{M}\Omega \approx 2\text{\mu A}$.
    *   $\Delta V = I \cdot \Delta t / C \implies C = I \cdot \Delta t / \Delta V$.
    *   $\Delta t = 1/f = 10\text{ms}$.
    *   $C = 2\text{\mu A} \cdot 10\text{ms} / 0.05\text{V} = 20\text{nF} \cdot 0.2 = 400\text{nF}$.
    *   $2.2\text{\mu F}$ should be plenty.

    *   Design 1: Standard P-SSHI.
    *   Design 2: P-SSHI with a larger inductor or different $t_{on}$ (though the optimizer handles values).
    *   Design 3: Try a "Voltage Doubler" (Dickson charge pump) instead of a bridge, but a bridge is more robust for AC. Wait, the reference was a bridge and it failed on voltage. A voltage doubler could increase $V_{out}$ but it's less efficient. Let's try a bridge with SSHI.

    *   D1: pzp -> out (DSCH)
    *   D2: pzn -> out (DSCH)
    *   D3: 0 -> pzp (DSCH)
    *   D4: 0 -> pzn (DSCH)
    *   L1: pzp -> n1
    *   S1: n1 -> pzn (ctrl: G1)
    *   G1: SYNC (ton=50u, phase=0, edges=both)
    *   C1: out -> 0 (2.2uF)

    *   What if $V_{out}$ goes too high (S3)?
    *   S3: $R_L = 10\text{M}\Omega$, $I_p = 120\text{uA}$.
    *   The power available is much higher.
    *   $P_{avail} \approx 0.5 \cdot 25\text{nF} \cdot (120/60 \cdot 3.8)^2 \cdot 100 \approx 72\text{\mu W}$.
    *   $P_{load} \approx 4.5^2 / 10\text{M} \approx 2\text{\mu W}$.
    *   With such a mismatch, $V_{out}$ will definitely exceed $5.5\text{V}$.
    *   We need a clamp. But we only have `DZ33` (3.3V).
    *   Can we use `DZ33` to clamp? No, $3.3\text{V} < 4.5\text{V}$.
    *   What if we use two `DZ33` in series? $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{V}$. That's too high ($> 5.5\text{V}$).
    *   What if we use a Zener in a different way?
    *   Actually, the only way to regulate the output without a Zener is to control the switching. But the SYNC controller is "ideal" and fixed to the piezo.
    *   Is there another way? Maybe a series resistor to drop voltage? No, that wastes power.
    *   Wait, maybe the "S3: strong excitation" condition is the trickiest. Let's look at the components again.
    *   Is there any other diode? `DSCH`, `DSI`, `DZ33`.
    *   Wait! If I use a `DZ33` as part of a regulator? No.
    *   What if I use the SYNC controller to "waste" energy if $V_{out}$ is too high? I can't, it's ideal.
    *   Let's reconsider the bridge. If I use a different rectifier?
    *   Actually, let's try the SSHI first. Maybe the optimizer will find a value for $L$ and $t_{on}$ that doesn't overcharge too quickly, or the $C_{out}$ will be large enough that it doesn't hit $5.5\text{V}$ within $0.8\text{s}$.
    *   Wait, $0.8\text{s}$ is not long. In S3, $P_{net} \approx 70\text{\mu W}$. $E = P \cdot t = 70\text{\mu W} \cdot 0.8\text{s} = 56\text{\mu J}$.
    *   $E_{cap} = 0.5 \cdot C \cdot V^2$. For $C = 2.2\text{\mu F}$ and $V = 5.5\text{V}$, $E_{cap} = 0.5 \cdot 2.2\cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 30.25 \approx 33\text{\mu J}$.
    *   So $V_{out}$ will definitely exceed $5.5\text{V}$ if $C_{out}$ is $2.2\text{\mu F}$ and $P_{net}$ is $70\text{\mu W}$.
    *   We need a larger $C_{out}$ to keep $V_{max}$ under $5.5\text{V}$.
    *   Let's try $C_{out} = 10\text{\mu F}$ or $22\text{\mu F}$.
    *   Max $C$ allowed is $4.7\text{\mu F}$.
    *   If $C = 4.7\text{\mu F}$, $E_{cap} = 0.5 \cdot 4.7\cdot 10^{-6} \cdot 30.25 \approx 71\text{\mu J}$.
    *   This is very close to the total energy $56\text{\mu J}$. So a $4.7\text{\mu F}$ capacitor might actually keep $V_{max} < 5.5\text{V}$ in S3.

    *   P-SSHI is the standard for this.
    *   Another option: a "Charge Pump" using the SYNC switches.
    *   But the simplest, most likely to work is P-SSHI.

    *   Let's propose two versions of SSHI:
        1.  Standard P-SSHI with a Full Bridge.
        2.  SSHI with a "Voltage Doubler" (using 2 capacitors and 2 diodes) to see if it handles the $4.5\text{V}$ target better. Actually, a bridge is generally more efficient. Let's try a bridge and a slightly different LC configuration.

    *   Wait, the problem says "at most 16 components". I'm only using 8.
    *   Let's refine Design 1 (P-SSHI).
    *   L1: 10mH, S1: 50us.

    *   Design 2: What if I use a "half-bridge" SSHI?
        *   Pzn connected to ground.
        *   L1, S1 between Pzp and Pzn.
        *   D1: pzp -> out.
        *   D2: out -> pzp (Wait, that's not right).
        *   A half-bridge only works if the piezo is AC-coupled. The piezo model here is a current source in parallel with $C_p$, which is inherently AC.
        *   But a full bridge is safer.

    *   Wait, the "Reference Design" used a Full Bridge and failed on $V_{out}$ (it was $3.3\text{V}$). This means the $V_{OC}$ was $3.8\text{V}$ and it lost $\sim 0.5\text{V}$ to the diodes. To get to $4.5\text{V}$, we *must* boost. SSHI is the most direct way.

    *   $L_1$ value: $10\text{mH}$ is a good start.
    *   $T_{on}$: $50\text{\mu s}$ is a good start.
    *   $C_{out}$: $4.7\text{\mu F}$ to minimize $V_{max}$ in S3.
    *   $D$: `DSCH` for lowest drop.

    *   The "Reference Design" failed `startup` and `settled`.
    *   `startup`: $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$.
    *   With SSHI, the voltage rises much faster.
    *   `settled`: $\Delta V \le 0.02\text{V}$.
    *   This requires the system to reach a steady state. With a large $C_{out}$, it might take longer, but the $0.8\text{s}$ window is the limit.

    *   Is there any other way to clamp?
    *   If $V_{out}$ exceeds $5.5\text{V}$, can I use a `DZ33` in series with a diode? $3.3 + 0.5 = 3.8\text{V}$. Still too low.
    *   Two `DZ33` in series? $6.6\text{V}$. Too high.
    *   A `DZ33` and a `DSCH`? No.
    *   What if I use a `DZ33` as a shunt but it only starts conducting at $3.3\text{V}$? That would clamp the output to $3.3\text{V}$, which is below the $4.5\text{V}$ minimum.
    *   So the only way to stay between $4.5\text{V}$ and $5.5\text{V}$ is to balance the energy harvested with the energy consumed by $R_L$.

    *   Let's double check the SYNC timing.
    *   $T_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    *   $L=10\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF} \to T_{on} \approx 50\text{\mu s}$.
    *   $L=1\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF} \to T_{on} \approx 15.7\text{\mu s}$.
    *   $L=100\text{\mu H}, C_p=25\text{nF} \to T_{on} \approx 5\text{\mu s}$.

    *   Let's provide one strong P-SSHI design.

    *   Wait, if I use `edges: "both"`, it flips at both peaks. This is the standard P-SSHI.
    *   If I use `edges: "pos"`, it only flips at the positive peak.
    *   `edges: "both"` is better.
